title: Grounding, citations, and the support gap
outcome: Distinguish source membership, claim support, freshness, and authority.
cue: A citation points. A support check proves a narrower claim.
version: Provider-neutral principles · Ruby 3.3 / Rails 7.2 lab · legacy Ruby 2.7 adaptation notes
useCase: Distinguish source membership, claim support, freshness, and authority.
benefits: A clear decision and a way to check it.
drawbacks: Citations can create false confidence. A correct number attached to the wrong category is still wrong. “All facts verified” is too strong if only IDs and numbers were checked.

trace.title: Claim and source ID
trace.detail:
## Understand

Grounding means relating an answer to supplied evidence. A good answer makes that relation inspectable: source identity, version/location, and the claim it supports.

Still ask four separate questions: was the source supplied, does it support this claim, is it current enough, and is it authoritative for this task?

Code can check many narrow facts exactly. A reported count can equal the supplied aggregate.

A claim about a rule code can match a verified rule result. A free-form explanation needs a different support check.

A source-ID membership validator cannot prove arbitrary prose is entailed by a passage.

Design partial or unavailable answers when evidence is incomplete or conflicting. Do not merge conflicting document revisions into a confident single instruction.

Keep generated interpretation visibly distinct from code-verified facts and reviewed guidance.

trace.title: Follow one input
trace.detail:
Extract claims → map to supplied source IDs → check exact fields where possible → assess semantic support → check freshness/authority → render the supported parts with clear labels.

Evaluate contradictions and misleading-but-valid citations explicitly.
